content: The provided text appears to be a detailed reference list and summary of studies, guidelines, and systematic reviews related to maternal and perinatal health, particularly focusing on the management of hypertension during pregnancy. 1. The 2018 edition of the WHO report on maternal mortality trends from 2000 to 2017, developed in collaboration with UNICEF, UNFPA, the World Bank Group, and the United Nations Population Division, provides comprehensive estimates and insights into global maternal health outcomes. This report was published by the World Health Organization in Geneva in 2019. 2. Yamin AE and Maine DP emphasized the importance of maternal mortality as a human rights issue, proposing methods to measure compliance with international treaty obligations. Their work was published in the Human Rights Quarterly in 1999 (Volume 21, Page 563). 3. The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights issued technical guidance on applying a human rights-based approach to policies and programs aimed at reducing preventable maternal morbidity and mortality. This guidance was presented during the 20th session of the Human Rights Council in New York in 2012. 4. Tunçalp Ö, Were W, MacLennan C, Oladapo O, Gülmezoglu A, Bahl R, and colleagues outlined the WHO vision for improving the quality of care for pregnant women and newborns. Their findings were published in BJOG in 2015 (Volume 122, Pages 1045-1049). 5. Campbell OM and Graham WJ, along with the Lancet Maternal Survival Series Steering Group, proposed evidence-based strategies for reducing maternal mortality, emphasizing the need to implement interventions that have proven effective. This work was published in The Lancet. 6. Fisk NM, McKee M, and Atun R analyzed the relative and absolute addressability of the global disease burden in maternal and perinatal health through targeted investments. Their findings were included in Tropical Medicine & International Health in 2011 (Volume 16, Pages 662-668). 7. Say L, Chou D, Gemmill A, Tunçalp Ö, Moller AB, Daniels J, and colleagues conducted a systematic analysis of global causes of maternal death, which was published in The Lancet Global Health in 2014 (Volume 2, Pages e323-e333). 8. The WHO released recommendations for the prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia in 2011, followed by updated guidelines on drug treatment for severe hypertension in pregnancy in 2018. Both documents were published in Geneva. 9. Abalos E, Cuesta C, Grosso AL, Chou D, and Say L conducted a systematic review to estimate the global and regional prevalence of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. Their findings were published in European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology in 2013 (Volume 170, Pages 1-7). 10. Abalos E, Cuesta C, Carroli G, Qureshi Z, Widmer M, Vogel J, and colleagues performed a secondary analysis of the WHO multicountry survey on maternal and newborn health, focusing on pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and associated adverse outcomes. This study was published in BJOG in 2014 (Volume 121, Pages 14-24). 11. Khan KS, Wojdyla D, Say L, Gülmezoglu AM, and Van Look PF conducted a systematic review of the causes of maternal death, which was published in The Lancet in 2006 (Volume 367, Pages 1066-1074). 12. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (Second Edition) was published in Geneva in 2014, providing a framework for developing evidence-based recommendations. 13. Vogel JP, Dowswell T, Lewin S, Bonet M, Hampson L, Kellie F, and colleagues introduced the concept of living guidelines for WHO recommendations on maternal and perinatal health. Their work was published in BMJ Global Health in 2019 (Volume 4, Article e001683). 14. The Executive Guideline Steering Group for updating WHO maternal and perinatal health recommendations (2017–2019) provided a comprehensive overview of the process and outcomes, available on the WHO website. 15. Abalos E, Duley L, Steyn DW, and Gialdini C reviewed the use of antihypertensive drug therapy for mild to moderate hypertension during pregnancy. Their systematic review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2018 (Issue 10). 16. Schünemann H, Brożek J, Guyatt G, and Oxman A authored a handbook for grading the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations using the GRADE approach, published in 2013. 17. Downie S, Finlayson K, Tunçalp Ö, and Gülmezoglu AM conducted a systematic scoping review to identify processes and outcomes of antenatal care that are important to healthy pregnant women. Their findings were published in BJOG in 2016 (Volume 123, Pages 529-539). 18. Downie S, Finlayson K, Tunçalp Ö, and Gülmezoglu AM synthesized qualitative evidence on the provision and uptake of routine antenatal services. This review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2019 (Issue 6). 19. The WHO published guidelines for managing complications in pregnancy and childbirth, specifically targeting midwives and doctors, in its second edition in 2017. 20. Standards for improving the quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities were released by the WHO in 2016. 21. Duffy J, Thompson T, Hinton L, Salinas M, McManus RJ, Ziebland S, and colleagues explored the outcomes that should be prioritized in pre-eclampsia research, based on the perspectives of women with lived experience. Their qualitative study was published in BJOG in 2019 (Volume 126, Pages 637-646). 22. Kayser A, Beck E, Hoeltzenbein M, Zinke S, Meister R, Weber-Schöndorfer C, and colleagues investigated the neonatal effects of intrauterine exposure to metoprolol or bisoprolol during the second and third trimesters. Their cohort study was published in the Journal of Hypertension in 2020 (Volume 38, Pages 354-361). 23. Arsenault C, Jordan K, Lee D, Dinsa G, Manzi F, Marchant T, and colleagues analyzed equity in antenatal care quality using data from 91 national household surveys. Their findings were published in The Lancet Global Health in 2018 (Volume 6, Pages e1186-e1195). 24. Persaud N, Jiang M, Shaikh R, Bali A, Oronsaye E, Woods H, and colleagues compared essential medicines lists across 137 countries. Their analysis was published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2019 (Volume 97, Pages 394-404). 25. The WHO has issued recommendations on drug treatment for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy, including assessments of beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, alpha-blockers, and other antihypertensive agents. These recommendations are based on systematic reviews and GRADE evaluations, highlighting the varying levels of evidence and priority for each intervention.
